gap: No result ChatGPT got states that a 15 A outdoor smart plug (Kasa EP40 or Minoston MP22Z, 1,875 W total) can carry only about 52% of the 3,600 W a 30 A RV pedestal delivers. It also doesn't say what the Wi-Fi Watchdog's extra cost buys per watt: $279.99 / 3,600 W = $0.078 per W for the PWD30EPOW, against $0.032 per W for the plain PWD30.
standout_why: Compared against the cited rival pages. The rvupgradestore PWD30EPOW page, cited in chat 2, already states the 3,600 W maximum load. The cited Hughes pages (hughesautoformers.com/power-watchdog-2nd-gen/ and /product/pwd30-epo/) now 301-redirect to powerwatchdog.com, which would not load (TLS certificate error), so I could not read their current text. ChatGPT's answer already says household smart plugs should not go between the pedestal and the RV, but only in words. No page puts the plug's capacity next to the 30 A service as a number, and none prices the Wi-Fi/EPO premium per watt or per amp.
decides: This confirms ChatGPT's split rather than changing the pick. A 15 A smart plug covers about half of a 30 A service, and the Kasa EP40 is rated for no more than a 1/2 HP motor. So it belongs on single appliances inside the RV, and the shore-power device should be a 30 A or 50 A Watchdog. On cost, the 50 A PWD50EPOW is about $8.00 per amp against $9.33 per amp for the 30 A PWD30EPOW, so it does not cost more per amp. The plain PWD30 at $114.49 costs about 41% of the PWD30EPOW's $279.99. What the extra $165.50 buys is Wi-Fi/Bluetooth app monitoring and kWh logging. For in-RV switching, Dealectric's Minoston MP22Z has the same 1,875 W rating as the Kasa EP40 at $26.35, which is $0.014 per W, but it needs a Z-Wave hub.
